title: Jonah's Anger and God's Question
summary: Jonah is furious that God spared Nineveh, and he finally explains why he ran: he knew God was gracious and compassionate and would relent. He asks to die, then waits outside the city to see what will happen. God appoints a plant to shade him, a worm to kill the plant, and a scorching wind, and when Jonah is angry about the plant, God asks whether he should not care about the great city of Nineveh, with its 120,000 people and many cattle.
story: Chapter 3 ended with the happiest outcome a prophet could hope for: a whole city repented and was spared. Chapter 4 reveals that this is the outcome Jonah feared from the beginning. The book's true climax is not the fish or the city but this conversation between God and his angry prophet. Everything so far (the flight, the storm, the psalm, the preaching) has been leading to the question Jonah raised by running and God raises by speaking: is it right for God to show mercy to people like the Ninevites? The book ends without Jonah's answer, leaving the question with the reader.
historical:
Jonah's anger makes sense against the history he knew. Assyria was the most feared military power of the day, and its kings boasted in their inscriptions of the cruelty they inflicted on rebels and conquered peoples. Within a few decades of Jeroboam II's reign, Assyria would destroy the northern kingdom of Israel, Jonah's own nation, and take Samaria in 722 BC. A prophet of Israel who suspected that a spared Nineveh would one day devour his people had real reasons for his dread. Nahum, a later prophet, would celebrate Nineveh's fall in 612 BC.

The figure of 120,000 people (verse 11) is a round number describing a great city. Whether it includes the whole population or only a part (for example, children, if "who cannot tell their right hand from their left" refers to young children) is debated. Either way, it describes a large and populous city by ancient standards.
cultural:
Jonah's prayer in verse 2 quotes Israel's central confession about God's character, first spoken by the LORD to Moses at Sinai after the golden calf: that he is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, and abounding in loving devotion (Exodus 34:6). This confession is echoed often in the Old Testament (Numbers 14:18, Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8, Nehemiah 9:17). Joel 2:13 uses the same wording, including the addition that God relents from sending disaster. Jonah recites the creed as a complaint.

The shelter Jonah builds east of the city (verse 5) is a sukkah, a temporary booth of branches, like those used at harvest and at the Feast of Booths. Such booths gave poor protection from the sun, so the plant God appoints to grow over it gives real relief. The plant's identity is uncertain; many suggest the castor-oil plant, a fast-growing shrub with broad leaves, while older translations guessed a gourd. The "scorching east wind" (verse 8) is the hot, dry wind from the desert, known today in the region by names such as sirocco or sharav, which can raise temperatures sharply and wither vegetation in a day.
literary: The chapter is built as a dialogue between God and Jonah framed by God's actions. Jonah prays (verses 2 and 3); God answers with a question (verse 4); Jonah withdraws; God acts through a plant, a worm, and a wind (verses 6 to 8); God asks the same question again (verse 9); Jonah answers defiantly; God speaks last (verses 10 and 11). The book ends with a question; among the prophets only Nahum does the same (Nahum 3:19), and Nahum's closing question is also aimed at Assyria. The verb "appointed" (manah) links this chapter to the fish of 1:17: God appoints a plant, a worm, and an east wind. Jonah's emotions swing from great displeasure (literally, it was evil to Jonah with a great evil) to great joy over the plant, echoing the book's repeated word "great". God's argument is from the lesser to the greater: if Jonah pities a plant he did not make, should God not pity a city of people and animals he did make?

outline.t: Jonah's angry prayer: I knew You were gracious
God's question: have you any right to be angry?
Jonah waits east of the city
God appoints a plant, a worm, and a scorching wind
The plant and the city: should I not care about Nineveh?

doctrines.note: Jonah's complaint is a creed: God is "a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion" (verse 2). The book shows these attributes at work toward the nations, and shows how offensive grace can be to those who think they deserve it more than others.

God's final question reveals his concern for the people of a foreign, violent city and even for their animals. God's compassion is not limited to his covenant people, and those who know his grace are meant to share his concern for others.

God's care extends to "many cattle as well" (verse 11). The Creator who made the plant, the worm, and the wind also cares for the animals of a city. His compassion covers everything he has made (Psalm 145:9).

words.note: Chus, to pity, spare, or have compassion. It often appears in idioms where the eye is the one that pities or refuses to pity (Deuteronomy 7:16). God uses it for Jonah's feeling for the plant (verse 10) and for his own concern for Nineveh (verse 11). The whole argument turns on this word: Jonah spares feeling for a plant but not for a city.

Charah, to burn with anger. Used four times of Jonah in this chapter. God's repeated question, "Have you any right to be angry?", uses the same verb. God does not simply rebuke the anger; he asks Jonah to examine it.

Manah, to appoint or assign. God appoints the fish (1:17), and here the plant, the worm, and the east wind. The repeated verb shows God directing every detail of Jonah's education, even through discomfort and loss.

Qiqayon, the plant. The word appears only in this chapter. Its identity is uncertain (castor-oil plant and gourd are the usual guesses). What matters is its short life: it sprang up in a night and perished in a night, and yet Jonah grieved it.

christ: Jonah quotes God's character as gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion. The Gospel of John says that in Jesus, the Word who became flesh, God's glory was seen "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14), language many interpreters connect with the same confession from Exodus 34:6. Where Jonah sat outside the city hoping to watch it destroyed, Jesus approached Jerusalem and wept over it (Luke 19:41). His parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32) also ends with an angry figure outside a celebration, the older brother who resents his father's mercy toward a sinner, and like Jonah it ends with the father's appeal and no recorded answer. The comparison is thematic rather than a prediction, but it shows that the question God asks Jonah is one Jesus kept asking.

hard.q: Why does the book end with a question and no answer from Jonah?
hard.a: The ending is deliberate. The book does not say whether Jonah repented of his anger, because the question is aimed past Jonah at the reader. Many interpreters think the first readers, whether Israelites in the eighth century or Judeans after the exile, were being asked to face their own resentment of God's mercy toward their enemies. Some suggest that the existence of the book, which portrays Jonah so unflatteringly, implies that Jonah or his circle later came to accept God's point. Others note that the question works best unanswered, leaving each reader to supply their own reply. Both readings agree that God's compassion is the last word, and that the question it raises is not answered by argument but by the reader's own heart.

questions: Jonah was angry because God was exactly who Jonah confessed him to be. Where does God's grace to others make you uncomfortable?
Jonah cared more about a plant that gave him comfort than a city full of people. What small comforts shape your emotions more than the needs of others?
The book ends with God's question. How would you answer it, and what would your answer require of you?
